-crL1-nZchk.title: How to Read a Federal Register Document | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome back to Federal Register Daily, the show where we help everyday people understand how federal rules get made. Today's episode is Rulemaking 101: How to Read a Federal Register Document. Every proposed rule and final rule follows the same required format, so once you know the pattern, you can read any document in the Federal Register. We'll walk through the rulebook that sets that format, then apply it to a real proposal from the State Department about passport renewal overseas. If you find this helpful, hit subscribe so you don't miss the next episode.

Let's start at the very top of any document. Federal rules follow a required preamble format written into the Code of Federal Regulations, at 1 CFR 18.12. It says each agency submitting a proposed or final rule document must prepare a preamble to inform the reader, who is not an expert in the subject area, of the basis and purpose for the rule or proposal. That's the whole point of this format. It's designed for you, not for lawyers. The document opens with AGENCY, which names the issuing agency, and ACTION, which tells you what kind of document this is: a notice, a proposed rule, or a final rule. Those two lines alone tell you who is acting and what stage the rulemaking is at.
Quick recap: Proposed and final rule documents start with AGENCY and ACTION, and the whole preamble is required to explain the rule in plain terms for non-experts.

Next comes the SUMMARY section, and this is often the most useful part for regular readers. The regulation requires brief statements, in simple language, of the action being taken, the circumstances which created the need for the action, and the intended effect of the action. In plain terms: what is the agency doing, why now, and what will change. If you only have thirty seconds to read a document, read the SUMMARY.
Quick recap: The SUMMARY section must plainly state what the agency is doing, why, and what effect it will have.

After the summary, look for DATES, ADDRESSES, and FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT. DATES tells you deadlines, like when comments are due or when a rule takes effect. ADDRESSES tells you where to send comments or find related documents. And for executive departments and agencies, the contact section gives the name and telephone number of a person in the agency to contact for additional information about the document. So if something in the rule confuses you, there is a person listed you can contact.
Quick recap: DATES gives deadlines, ADDRESSES tells you where to respond, and the contact section names a person you can reach.

The last major section is SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION, and it is usually the longest part. Agencies are allowed to include a discussion of the background and major issues involved, and in a final rule, any significant differences from the proposed version, plus a response to substantive public comments. This is where you will find the agency's full reasoning, the history of the issue, and how it responded to what the public told them. It is dense, but it is where the real explanation lives.
Quick recap: SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION holds the background, the reasoning, and the agency's responses to public comments.

Now, why does any of this matter legally? Under federal law, 44 U.S.C. 1507, a document required to be published is not valid as against a person who has not had actual knowledge of it until the document has been filed with the Office of the Federal Register and a copy made available for public inspection. The same law says filing a document with the Office of the Federal Register is generally sufficient to give notice of its contents to people affected by it. And publication creates a rebuttable presumption that the document was duly issued and that the printed copy is a true copy of the original. That is why this daily journal matters so much.
Quick recap: Filing with the Federal Register generally gives legal notice, and publication creates a rebuttable presumption that the document was properly issued.

Let's put this to work on a real document. The State Department published a proposed rule titled Passports: Expanding Online Passport Renewal Overseas. Its SUMMARY section tells us the Department proposes expanding online passport application availability to qualified applicants located in foreign countries. Reading further into SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION, State explained why: the online process allows the applicant to bypass the logistical hurdle of securing appointments, which State said has often been a challenge for citizens residing abroad. That is the basis and purpose the preamble format is designed to give you, right there in plain language.
Quick recap: The State Department's SUMMARY told readers exactly what the rule does, expanding online passport renewal to people overseas, and why.

Finally, check the DATES section to find out how to take part. This proposal says the Department of State will accept comments until October 27, 2026. As of September 13, Regulations.gov listed four public comments. If this passport proposal affects you or someone you know living abroad, you can go to regulations.gov, find this docket, and submit your own comment before the deadline.
Quick recap: This proposal's comment deadline is October 27, 2026, and Regulations.gov listed four comments as of September 13.

Thanks for spending time with us on Federal Register Daily. Now you know how to open any Federal Register document and find what it does, why, when to comment, and who to call. Subscribe so you catch the next episode of Rulemaking 101, and leave a comment telling us which section you find hardest to read. And take a look at the passport renewal proposal or any other open rule on regulations.gov. Your comment becomes part of the official record.

IpDmCPenY2g.title: How a Federal Rule Is Made: The Rulemaking Process | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome back to Federal Register Daily, the show where we turn the federal rulebook into plain English. I'm your host, and today we're doing something special. We're walking you through the entire life of a federal rule, from idea to law, using a real VA rule about digestive system disability ratings as our case study. You'll learn where the public gets to weigh in, what happens to your comments, and how Congress gets a final check on big rules. If you're new here, hit subscribe so you never miss an episode. Let's get into it.

Most federal rules start the same way, with a proposed rule. Under the law that governs rulemaking, 5 U.S. Code Section 553, agencies generally have to tell the public what they're planning before it becomes final. The statute says, quote, General notice of proposed rule making shall be published in the Federal Register, unless persons subject thereto are named. That notice has to include the time, place, and nature of the proceedings, the legal authority behind the rule, and the terms or a summary of what's being proposed. This is step one, and it's your first chance to find out a rule is coming. The Federal Register comes out every business day, and anyone can read it for free. Think of this notice as the government's rough draft, posted publicly so you can react before it's locked in.
Quick recap: in the standard process, the agency first publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register explaining what it wants to do and why.

Let's see this in action. In January 2022, the Department of Veterans Affairs published a proposed rule to update its Schedule for Rating Disabilities for the digestive system. As VA put it, quote, These changes add medical conditions not currently in the rating schedule, revise the rating criteria to reflect medical advances, clarify existing rating criteria, and update medical terminology. VA also said it considered the most up-to-date medical knowledge and clinical practice of gastroenterology. VA set a deadline: comments were due by March 14, 2022. That's the window where veterans, advocacy groups, doctors, and anyone else could go to regulations.gov and tell VA what they thought. Regulations.gov lists 22 public comments on this proposal. And as we'll see next, comments can actually change the final rule.
Quick recap: VA proposed updated digestive system disability ratings in January 2022 and gave the public until March 2022 to comment, and Regulations.gov lists 22 comments.

So what happens to those comments? This is where Section 553 comes back in. The law says, quote, After consideration of the relevant matter presented, the agency shall incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose. In plain terms, the agency can't just ignore what people say. It has to actually consider the comments and then explain, in the final rule, how it responded. This is the heart of notice-and-comment rulemaking. It's not a public vote, but it is a real conversation. Sometimes agencies keep the language the same. Sometimes a single well-placed comment leads to a real change in the final text, which is exactly what happened with the VA digestive rule.
Quick recap: after the comment period closes, the law requires the agency to consider the comments and explain its reasoning in the final rule.

Two years later, in March 2024, VA published its final rule on digestive system ratings, effective May 19, 2024. The final rule includes a long, detailed response to public comments, issue by issue. For example, on esophagus stricture ratings, a commenter pointed out an inconsistency in the draft criteria. VA responded directly, saying, quote, VA agrees and revises the 30% criteria to only include recurrent esophageal strictures while the 50 percent criteria will reference both recurrent and refractory esophageal strictures. That's a real, specific change made because someone caught a problem and wrote in about it. Not every comment led to a change. On speech impairment after loss of the tongue, VA made one change commenters asked for and declined another, explaining that speech is not a function of the digestive body system. Either way, the final rule shows VA's reasoning, comment by comment.
Quick recap: in its March 2024 final rule, VA walked through public comments one by one, making some changes and explaining why it declined to make others.

Notice something about the timing here. VA published its final rule on March 20, 2024, and made it effective on May 19, 2024, exactly 60 days later. Section 553 sets the usual minimum, quote, The required publication or service of a substantive rule shall be made not less than 30 days before its effective date. But VA said this rule may have an annual effect on the economy of 100 million dollars or more, so it is subject to the 60-day delay under the Congressional Review Act. We'll come back to that in a moment. Either way, the gap gives people time to prepare before a new rule kicks in. For veterans and VA staff, it meant time to get ready for the new digestive system rating criteria before it applied to real cases.
Quick recap: the law usually requires at least 30 days between publication and the effective date, and major rules like this one wait at least 60 days.

There's one more check built into the system, especially for big rules. Under 5 U.S. Code Section 801, part of the Congressional Review Act, the law says, quote, Before a rule can take effect, the Federal agency promulgating such rule shall submit to each House of the Congress and to the Comptroller General a report. That report has to include a copy of the rule, a statement of whether it's a major rule, and its proposed effective date. This gives Congress a window to review new rules and, if lawmakers choose, pass a joint resolution of disapproval. It's a safety valve that sits on top of everything you just learned.
Quick recap: before a rule takes effect, the agency must report it to Congress and the Comptroller General, giving lawmakers a chance to review it.

So what makes a rule major? Section 804 gives the definition. A major rule is one likely to cause, quote, an annual effect on the economy of $100,000,000 or more, or a major increase in costs, or significant harm to competition. That threshold matters. For the digestive system rule, VA said it may result in an annual effect on the economy of 100 million dollars or more, so it is subject to the 60-day delay in effective date under Section 801. That's why it took effect 60 days after publication.
Quick recap: a rule likely to have a 100 million dollar annual effect on the economy, among other tests, is a major rule, and major rules wait at least 60 days to take effect.

That's the full journey: proposed rule, public comments, agency response, final rule, effective date, and congressional review. Thanks for spending this time with us here on Federal Register Daily. If this helped, please subscribe so you catch every episode. Tell us in the comments, have you ever submitted a comment on a proposed rule, or is there a rule you'd like us to break down next? And keep an eye on regulations.gov, there are open proposed rules right now waiting for your voice.

LIpoeXO8yHY.title: Interim Final and Direct Final Rules: The Fast Track | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome back to Rulemaking 101 here on Federal Register Daily. Most rules go through notice and comment: a proposal, a comment period, then a final rule. But today we're looking at two shortcuts agencies use: interim final rules and direct final rules. You'll learn why agencies use them, and how you can still have a say. If that sounds useful, hit subscribe so you don't miss the next episode.

Let's start with the law itself. The Administrative Procedure Act says agencies must publish general notice of a proposed rule and give interested persons an opportunity to submit comments. But there's an exception. The law says an agency can skip that step if it finds, for good cause, that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. When an agency uses this good cause exception, it has to explain its reasoning right in the rule. This exception is the legal basis for what's called an interim final rule.
Quick recap: the good cause exception lets an agency skip advance notice and comment if doing so would be impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest, as long as it explains why.

Here's that good cause exception in action. In September 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services issued an interim final rule pausing registration for certain insurance agents and brokers who help people enroll through the federal health insurance exchanges. HHS finds good cause under the Administrative Procedure Act to waive prior notice and comment. HHS said advance notice would be contrary to the public interest and impracticable, tied to concerns about fraud, waste, and abuse in enrollment activity. The rule took effect right away, on September 22, 2026. But HHS still invited public comments, to be assured consideration by November 21, 2026, and said it would consider them in deciding whether to retain, modify, or rescind this authority. As of September 25, Regulations.gov listed 40 public comments.
Quick recap: HHS made this rule effective immediately using the good cause exception, but still opened a comment period afterward, with comments due November 21, 2026.

There's a second piece of this puzzle. Normally a substantive rule can't take effect until at least 30 days after it's published. But the law allows an exception here too: that 30-day wait doesn't apply as otherwise provided by the agency for good cause found and published with the rule. That's exactly what let the HHS rule become effective immediately upon publication, instead of waiting the usual 30 days. So interim final rules like this one rely on two good cause findings from this same statute: one to skip the comment period, and one to skip the 30-day delay.
Quick recap: a separate good cause finding lets an agency start a rule right away instead of waiting the usual 30 days, which is why interim final rules can take effect immediately.

Now let's look at a different fast track: the direct final rule. Agencies use this when they expect a change to be noncontroversial. In September 2026, the USDA published a direct final rule simplifying language about buying local food for school lunches and other child nutrition programs. USDA said the changes don't alter the meaning of the regulations or their implementation, they just clarify existing rules. The rule sets its own trigger: this rule will become effective on November 9, 2026, unless the Department receives written adverse comments on or before October 9, 2026. So instead of comments coming after the rule takes effect, like with HHS, here comments during that window can actually stop the rule from taking effect. As of September 19, Regulations.gov listed 2 comments on this one.
Quick recap: a direct final rule sets a future effective date unless the agency receives adverse comments by the deadline; USDA's deadline is October 9, 2026.

So what happens when someone does push back? Here's an example. In July 2026, the Consumer Product Safety Commission published a direct final rule to remove two outdated rules about infant bouncer seats and stationary activity centers, saying those products are now covered by newer, more comprehensive safety standards. But in September 2026, the Commission reversed course. The Commission received a significant adverse comment concerning the direct final rule and thus is withdrawing the direct final rule. The Commission said it will consider the significant adverse comment and assess the appropriate manner in which to proceed. This shows the safety valve built into direct final rules: if the agency hears real objections in time, the rule doesn't just quietly take effect.
Quick recap: because CPSC received a significant adverse comment, it withdrew its direct final rule instead of letting it take effect, showing how public comments can actually stop this kind of rule.

Thanks for learning with us today. Interim final and direct final rules move fast, but they're not closed doors: you can still comment, and as the CPSC example shows, a single comment can change the outcome. Subscribe so you catch the next episode, drop a comment with your own question or experience, and take a look at open proposed rules on regulations.gov where your voice can make a difference. See you next time on Federal Register Daily.

MDOurHcaBbA.title: Make Your Public Comment More Useful: Be Specific | FedReg Intel
transcript: This is FedReg Intel. Want to make a public comment more useful? Say what should change, explain why, and offer a practical alternative. This is an evergreen writing tip, not today's news. Start by reading the proposal and its instructions.

EPA recommends specific suggestions supported by examples and reasoning. Instead of only saying a proposal is burdensome, identify the provision you mean and describe the effect on you. Explain relevant experience without claiming expertise you do not have.

Here is a hypothetical example, not an actual rule: A proposed monthly report would repeat information already submitted each quarter. Identify the repeated fields, explain the time involved, and suggest reusing the existing report. Support your estimate rather than inventing numbers.

You can also explain which parts you support and why. Organize separate concerns under headings. EPA emphasizes reasoning and evidence over counting votes. A thoughtful comment does not guarantee your preferred result.
Read the official guidance linked below. For more help, find How to Comment on Federal Rules at FedReg Intel dot com. Educational information, not legal advice.

QLM-K-VpsHo.title: The Congressional Review Act: How Congress Can Overturn a Rule | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome back to Federal Register Daily. This is Rulemaking 101, the series that helps everyday people understand how federal rules get made, and sometimes unmade. Today we're looking at the Congressional Review Act, or CRA. This is the law that lets Congress vote to cancel a federal rule after an agency finalizes it. By the end of this video, you'll know how that process works, what counts as a major rule, and we'll walk through two real Federal Register documents, from 2025 and 2026, where agencies removed rules after Congress disapproved them. If you're new here, go ahead and subscribe so you don't miss the next episode.

Let's start with the basics. Under the law, before most rules can take effect, the agency has to submit them to Congress first. The statute says the agency must send a report to both the House and the Senate, and to the Comptroller General. That report includes a copy of the rule, a statement about whether it's a major rule, and the date it's supposed to take effect. This is what opens the window for Congress to review the rule at all. The window for introducing a disapproval resolution is tied to when Congress receives this report.
Quick recap: before a rule takes effect, the agency has to send Congress a report describing the rule and its effective date.

So how does Congress actually reject a rule? Through a joint resolution of disapproval. The law spells out the exact wording lawmakers use, filling in the agency name and the rule. If both the House and Senate pass that resolution and the President signs it, the rule has no force or effect. The Senate process is expedited too. Under the statute, debate is limited to ten hours, and if a committee hasn't acted after 20 calendar days, a petition supported in writing by 30 senators can discharge it. This is why CRA resolutions can move faster than typical legislation.
Quick recap: Congress can pass a joint resolution disapproving a rule, using expedited Senate procedures, and if the President signs it, the rule has no force or effect.

You'll hear the term major rule a lot with the CRA, so let's define it. The law says a rule is major if the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs finds it's likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100,000,000 or more, or a major increase in costs for consumers or industries, or significant effects on things like competition or employment. Major rules get extra scrutiny, including a report from the Comptroller General, and they take effect on a delayed timeline so Congress has time to review them.
Quick recap: a major rule is one likely to have at least a $100 million effect on the economy, or major cost increases, or significant competitive effects.

Here's a detail that surprises a lot of people. Once Congress disapproves a rule, the agency doesn't just lose that one rule. The statute says the rule may not be reissued in substantially the same form, and a new rule that is substantially the same as such a rule may not be issued. There's an exception: Congress could pass a later law specifically authorizing it. But absent that, the agency is largely blocked from bringing back a similar rule on its own.
Quick recap: once disapproved, a rule can't be reissued in substantially the same form unless a later law specifically allows it.

Now let's see this play out in real life. The IRS and Treasury Department had finalized a rule requiring certain digital asset brokers to report gross proceeds. According to this Federal Register document, the House passed a joint resolution disapproving that rule on March 11, 2025, the Senate passed it on March 26, and the President signed it on April 10, 2025, as Public Law 119-5. The document states that under Public Law 119-5 and by operation of the CRA, the Final Rule has no force or effect. So the IRS removed the rule from the Code of Federal Regulations and reverted to the text in effect before it. The document notes that under the CRA, a rule disapproved this way is treated as though it had never taken effect.
Quick recap: Congress disapproved the IRS digital asset broker rule, the President signed the resolution, and the IRS removed the rule from the CFR.

Here's a second example, this time from the EPA. In 2024, EPA finalized new air emissions standards for the rubber processing part of tire manufacturing. This document explains that Congress passed a joint resolution disapproving that rule, with the Senate passing it on May 6, 2025, and the President signed it on May 23, 2025, as Public Law 119-14. The document says that under the joint resolution and by operation of the CRA, the 2024 Rubber Tire Rule has no legal force or effect. So EPA removed those provisions and reverted to the earlier 2020 rule that had been in place before.
Quick recap: Congress disapproved EPA's 2024 rubber tire emissions rule, and EPA reverted to the earlier 2020 standards.

That's the Congressional Review Act in a nutshell: agencies report rules to Congress, Congress can vote to disapprove them through an expedited process, and once disapproved, a rule loses its force and generally can't come back in a similar form. Thanks for learning with us today. Subscribe for more episodes of Rulemaking 101, and tell us in the comments about a rule you've followed or a question you still have. And remember, you can always go read and comment on open proposed rules yourself at regulations.gov.

RMJT7vvNL9w.title: VA Disability Compensation Rules: How Public Comments Shape Them | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome to Federal Register Daily, part of our Rulemaking 101 series. Today we're talking about VA disability compensation rules, the rules that decide how much veterans get paid for service-connected conditions. We'll look at a real interim final rule that took effect immediately, why it drew so many public comments, and why VA rescinded it just ten days later. Then we'll walk through a standard rulemaking example, so you can see how a proposal becomes a final rule after comments come in. If this is your first time here, hit subscribe so you don't miss how these rules affect real benefits.

VA's disability ratings come from something called the Schedule for Rating Disabilities, or VASRD. It lives in Title 38 of the Code of Federal Regulations, part 4, and VA updates it through rulemaking, the same public process we cover every episode. In February 2026, VA used that process to change one of its core rules, section 4.10, about how examiners judge a veteran's functional impairment. VA said the amendment clarifies that veterans should be compensated for the actual level of functional impairment they experience, and that the ameliorative effects of medication should not be estimated or discounted when evaluating the severity of a veteran's disability at the time of the exam. In other words, VA wanted veterans rated on the impairment they actually have, with treatment, rather than on an estimate of how severe it would be without treatment.
Quick recap: VA's disability ratings live in 38 CFR part 4, and in February 2026 VA changed a core rule about how medication affects a veteran's rating.

Why the rush? VA pointed to a court decision, Ingram versus Collins, decided in 2025. VA said the regulation was needed immediately to minimize the negative impact of an erroneous line of cases culminating in the recent decision of Ingram v. Collins. VA warned that Ingram could touch over 500 diagnostic codes and force re-adjudication of more than 350,000 pending claims. Because VA said the rule was needed immediately, it used a special tool: an interim final rule, which skips the usual comment-first step and takes effect right away.
Quick recap: VA said a 2025 court decision, Ingram v. Collins, threatened hundreds of thousands of pending claims, so it acted immediately instead of waiting for comments first.

That's the key difference from a normal proposed rule. Normally you comment before a rule takes effect. Here, the interim final rule took effect February 17, 2026, the day it was published, and VA accepted comments until April 20, 2026. So the change to section 4.10 was already the law the day it published, and the public was invited to comment afterward. And comment they did. As of April 10, 2026, Regulations.gov showed 20,880 public comments on this single rule, a huge response.
Quick recap: this rule took effect the day it was published, with comments accepted afterward, and Regulations.gov lists 20,880 public comments.

Ten days after the rule took effect, VA reversed course. On February 27, 2026, VA published a final rule rescinding the interim rule and restoring the prior text of section 4.10. VA explained what happened, saying VA always takes veterans' concerns seriously and recognizes that many commenters construed the interim final rule as something that could result in adverse consequences. VA skipped notice and comment for the rescission too. It said leaving the rule in place during a lengthy rulemaking could undermine confidence in the benefits system, and that the rescission restores the prior text to maintain stability without resolving the legal questions now before the courts.
Quick recap: VA rescinded the rule just ten days later, noting that many commenters saw it as something that could result in adverse consequences, and restored the prior text.

Now let's see what a standard VA rulemaking looks like, from start to finish, using the Digestive System rule. In January 2022, VA proposed changes to sections 4.110 through 4.114. The proposal would add medical conditions not currently in the rating schedule, revise the rating criteria to reflect medical advances that have occurred since the last revision, clarify existing rating criteria, and update medical terminology. VA gave the public until March 14, 2022 to comment, and Regulations.gov lists 22 comments on that proposal.
Quick recap: VA proposed updates to the digestive system ratings in 2022, based on medical advances, and the public had until March 14 to weigh in.

Two years later, in March 2024, VA published the final rule, effective May 19, 2024. And you can see comments actually changing the outcome. On stricture of the esophagus, one commenter pointed out a mismatch in how often dilatation treatments were required at different rating levels. VA responded, VA agrees and revises the 30% criteria to only include recurrent esophageal strictures while the 50% criteria will reference both recurrent and refractory esophageal strictures. That's the process working as intended: a comment catches a problem, and the final rule fixes it.

Today we're answering one of the most searched questions about government: who writes the rules that affect your daily life? We'll look at the law that defines what counts as a rule and an agency, how the Federal Register publishes those rules, how they end up in the Code of Federal Regulations, and we'll walk through a real proposed rule from USDA about importing birds, so you can see the whole process in action. If you want more explainers like this, hit subscribe so you don't miss an episode.

Let's start with the basics. Congress writes the big laws, but it's federal agencies that write the detailed rules that put those laws into action. The law that defines these terms is 5 U.S. Code Section 551. It says a rule means an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy. In plain English, a rule is a written statement from an agency that tells people what the law requires going forward. The same law defines rule making simply as agency process for formulating, amending, or repealing a rule. And an agency, under this law, is basically any authority of the U.S. government, though it specifically excludes Congress itself and the courts. So when you hear about a new federal rule, remember: Congress passed the underlying law, but an executive branch agency, not Congress, wrote the actual rule you're reading.
Quick recap: Congress passes laws, and agencies write the specific rules that carry those laws out, as defined in 5 U.S.C. 551.

So once an agency writes a rule, how does it become public? That's where the Office of the Federal Register comes in. Under 44 U.S. Code Section 1502, the Archivist of the United States, acting through the Office of the Federal Register, is charged with the custody and, together with the Director of the Government Publishing Office, with the prompt and uniform publishing of the documents. In other words, this office, working with the Government Publishing Office, is responsible for making sure federal documents are published consistently so the public can find them. A director, appointed by the Archivist, runs this office day to day. Think of the Office of the Federal Register as the official record keeper and publisher for every rule the government issues. Without it, there would be no single place for the public to see what rules agencies are proposing or finalizing.
Quick recap: The Office of the Federal Register, under the Archivist, is in charge of publishing the documents that the law requires.

Not every government document ends up in the Federal Register, so what exactly has to be published there? 44 U.S. Code Section 1505 spells it out. It requires publication of presidential proclamations and executive orders with general effect, documents the President determines have general applicability, and documents or classes of documents that may be required so to be published by Act of Congress. So if Congress specifically requires a type of document to be published, it has to appear in the Federal Register. This matters because it's the Federal Register where proposed and final rules are officially announced, which is also where the public comment process begins. If a rule never gets published there, the public wouldn't have an official, searchable record of it.
Quick recap: Federal law requires certain documents, including rules with legal effect, to be published in the Federal Register so the public can see them.

Once a rule is finalized and published in the Federal Register, it doesn't just disappear into a daily newspaper of government action. It gets organized into a permanent reference book. 44 U.S. Code Section 1510 explains that the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register can require a complete codification of the documents of each agency of the Government having general applicability and legal effect. transcript: Welcome back to Rulemaking 101. Today we are talking about a law with a long name but a simple goal: the Regulatory Flexibility Act. It is the law that tells federal agencies, hey, before you write a rule, think about the small businesses, nonprofits, and small local governments who will have to follow it. We will walk through the key definitions, the analyses agencies must do, a shortcut agencies can sometimes use, and how old rules get a second look. Then we will check out a current FCC proposal that affects small phone and internet providers. If you want more plain English guides to how Washington makes rules, hit subscribe so you never miss an episode.

First, who counts as a small entity under this law. The statute, 5 U.S. Code section 601, lays out three groups. A small business generally means a small business concern under the Small Business Act, though agencies can set their own definition after public comment. A small organization is a not-for-profit that is independently owned and operated and not dominant in its field. And a small governmental jurisdiction means, in the law's own words, governments of cities, counties, towns, townships, villages, school districts, or special districts, with a population of less than fifty thousand. So if you run a small nonprofit, a mom and pop shop, or sit on a small town council, this law is built with you in mind.
Quick recap: small entities include certain small businesses, small nonprofits, and local governments serving under fifty thousand people.

Now that we know who counts, here is what agencies have to do before finalizing most rules. Under 5 U.S. Code section 603, when an agency proposes a rule, it must prepare an initial regulatory flexibility analysis. That analysis has to include a description of and, where feasible, an estimate of the number of small entities to which the proposed rule will apply. It also has to explain why the agency is acting, describe expected paperwork and compliance costs, and flag any other federal rules that might overlap. Importantly, the law says agencies must discuss significant alternatives that would lessen the burden on small entities, like different timelines, simpler paperwork, or even an exemption. This analysis is published alongside the proposed rule, so the public can react to it.
Quick recap: before finalizing a rule, agencies must estimate the impact on small entities and spell out less burdensome alternatives.

After the comment period closes, the agency has more homework. Section 604 requires a final regulatory flexibility analysis. It must include a statement of any changes made in the proposed rule as a result of such comments. In plain terms, the agency has to tell you whether your comments, or anyone else's, actually changed the final rule, and why. It also has to respond to any comments filed by the Small Business Administration's Chief Counsel for Advocacy, including a detailed statement of any changes made to the final rule as a result of those comments, and it must describe the steps it took to minimize the rule's economic impact on small entities, including the reasons for selecting the alternative it adopted and why each other significant alternative was rejected. This is where your comment can leave a real paper trail, showing up in the government's own explanation of its final decision.
Quick recap: the final analysis has to say whether comments changed the rule, giving your input a documented place in the process.

Not every rule triggers all that analysis. Section 605 lets an agency skip sections 603 and 604 if the head of the agency certifies that the rule will not, if promulgated, have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If an agency makes that certification, it still has to publish it in the Federal Register along with the facts behind that conclusion, and send it to the Small Business Administration's Chief Counsel for Advocacy. So when you see a rule with no regulatory flexibility analysis, look for this certification. It is the agency's way of saying, we checked, and this one will not hit small entities hard.
Quick recap: agencies can skip the detailed analysis by certifying, with a stated factual basis, that small entities will not be significantly affected.

The Regulatory Flexibility Act does not stop once a rule is final. Section 610 requires agencies to periodically review existing rules that have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. As the law puts it, the purpose of the review shall be to determine whether such rules should be continued without change, or should be amended or rescinded. Agencies look at factors such as the continued need for the rule, the nature of complaints or comments received concerning the rule from the public, and the extent to which the rule overlaps, duplicates, or conflicts with other federal rules. Each year, agencies publish a list of rules up for this review, and that list invites public comment too.
Quick recap: agencies must periodically revisit rules that burden small entities and ask whether to keep, change, or cancel them.

Let's see all this in action. The FCC has a proposed rule open right now about its Robocall Mitigation Database, the system that tracks which phone and internet voice providers are following rules against illegal robocalls. The FCC wants to clarify which entities must file in that database, including smaller providers like VoIP resellers and mobile virtual network operators, and it wants tighter screening to keep bad actors out. Quick recap: the FCC's robocall database proposal affects small providers too, and comments close October 9, 2026, with replies due November 9.

That is the Regulatory Flexibility Act in a nutshell: agencies must think about small businesses, nonprofits, and small governments before and after they write a rule. transcript: Welcome back to Federal Register Daily, the show where we make rulemaking make sense. Today we're answering a big question: once a final rule is published, when does it actually start applying to you? We'll look at the general 30 day rule, what Congress added with the Congressional Review Act, and how interim final rules can take effect right away. We'll use real examples from VA and the Coast Guard so you can see how this plays out in practice. If you're new here, hit subscribe so you don't miss the next episode.

Let's start with the basic rule. Under a law called 5 U.S.C. 553, once an agency finishes a rule, it generally has to publish it at least 30 days before the rule takes effect. That gap gives people time to read the rule, adjust their plans, or figure out how it affects them. But the law also lists exceptions. A rule that grants an exemption or relieves a restriction doesn't need the 30 day wait. Interpretive rules and policy statements are excluded too. And an agency can shorten the wait if it finds, quote, good cause, and explains that reason publicly in the rule itself. So the 30 day window is the default, not an absolute rule.
Quick recap: final rules usually need at least 30 days between publication and taking effect, but the law allows exceptions when an agency has good cause.

Now let's talk about a special category called a major rule. Congress defined this term in 5 U.S.C. 804. A rule counts as major if the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs finds it's likely to have an annual effect on the economy of 100 million dollars or more, or a major increase in costs for consumers or industries, or significant harm to competition or innovation. This label matters because major rules get extra scrutiny before they can take effect, which we'll explain next.
Quick recap: a major rule is one expected to have a big economic impact, like a 100 million dollar effect on the economy, and that label triggers extra review.

Here's where the Congressional Review Act comes in, found in 5 U.S.C. 801. Before any rule can take effect, the agency must report it to Congress. But for major rules specifically, the law says the rule takes effect on the latest of several dates, generally 60 days after Congress receives the report or the rule is published, whichever is later. This gives lawmakers a window to review major rules and, if they choose, pass a joint resolution of disapproval. So for major rules, that 60 day clock can stretch the timeline well beyond the basic 30 day rule we just covered.
Quick recap: major rules generally can't take effect until at least 60 days after Congress gets the report or the rule is published, giving lawmakers time to review it.

Let's see a major rule in action. VA published a final rule updating how it rates digestive system disabilities on March 20, 2024. Its Dates section said the rule was effective May 19, 2024, exactly 60 days later. Why 60 and not 30? VA said this rule may result in an annual effect on the economy of 100 million dollars or more, so it is subject to the 60-day delay in effective date under the Congressional Review Act. VA said the changes were meant to use current medical terminology and give more detailed criteria for evaluating digestive conditions. When you read a final rule, look for that Dates line. It tells you exactly when the new requirements start.
Quick recap: the VA digestive system rule was a major rule, so it took effect 60 days after it was published.

Now compare that to an interim final rule. VA published a rule about how medication affects disability evaluations, and its Dates section says the rule is effective February 17, 2026, the same day it was published. That's allowed because 553 lets an agency skip the waiting period for good cause. VA explained it needed the change immediately to address a court decision it said could force re-adjudication of over 350,000 pending claims. Here's the key part for you as a viewer: even though this rule took effect immediately, VA still accepted public comments, with a deadline of April 20, 2026. So an interim final rule starts working right away, but the public conversation isn't over. As of April 10, 2026, Regulations.gov showed 20,880 comments. And ten days after it took effect, on February 27, 2026, VA rescinded the rule, which we cover in our VA episode.
Quick recap: interim final rules can take effect immediately for good cause, like this VA medication rule, while the agency still takes public comments afterward.

Last example, and it's a short-lived one. The Coast Guard set up a temporary safety zone in Zach's Bay, New York, for a triathlon swim event. The rule's Dates section gives a specific window, effective from 6 a.m. on September 25, 2026, through 4 p.m. the next day, with enforcement only during set hours each day. The Coast Guard said it had good cause to skip both the normal comment period and the 30 day waiting period, because the rule needed to be in place before the event started. This shows that some final rules aren't permanent at all. They're built for a defined window of time, and the Dates section tells you exactly when that window opens and closes.
Quick recap: this Coast Guard rule used good cause to take effect quickly and only lasted for a short, specific window tied to one event.

That's it for today. Thanks for learning with us here on Federal Register Daily. Next time you see a rule, check its Dates section first, it tells you the whole story, whether it's a standard 30 day wait, a major rule under congressional review, or an interim rule already in effect. u2XFLMZk1TA.title: What Is the Administrative Procedure Act? | Rulemaking 101
transcript: Welcome back to Federal Register Daily. I'm your host, and today we're talking about the law that makes all of this possible: the Administrative Procedure Act, or APA. It's the rulebook agencies have to follow when they make rules that affect you. By the end of this episode, you'll know what counts as a rule, how the public comment process works, when agencies can skip steps, and how courts check agency power. We'll also look at a real VA rule to see this law in action. If you're new here, hit subscribe so you never miss how Washington makes its rules.

Let's start with the basics. What is a rule, legally speaking? Under 5 U.S.C. 551, a rule is an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy. In plain terms, it's a decision an agency makes now that will apply going forward, whether to everyone in an industry or to a narrower group. And rule making is just the process agencies use to write, change, or cancel those rules. This definition matters because it's the trigger. If something counts as a rule, other parts of the APA kick in.
Quick recap: a rule is an agency statement with future effect that implements or interprets law or policy, and rule making is the process of creating or changing it.

So how does an agency actually make a rule? Section 553 of the APA says general notice of proposed rule making shall be published in the Federal Register, unless persons subject thereto are named and personally served. That notice has to include the time, place, and nature of the proceedings, the legal authority behind it, and either the actual proposed text or a description of the issues involved. This is the 'notice' half of notice-and-comment. It's why every proposed rule you see on our channel starts with a Federal Register publication.
Quick recap: agencies must publish notice of a proposed rule in the Federal Register, spelling out what it covers and under what legal authority.

After notice, the public gets to weigh in. Section 553 says agencies must give interested persons an opportunity to participate through written data, views, or arguments. Then, after considering the relevant matter presented, the agency shall incorporate in the rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose. That statement is the agency's explanation of why it made the choices it did, and it's supposed to reflect that comments were actually considered, not just collected.
Quick recap: after taking comments, the agency must explain, in a concise statement, the basis and purpose behind the final rule.

Notice-and-comment doesn't always happen first. Section 553 lets an agency skip it when, for good cause, it finds that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. This is often called the 'good cause exception.' The agency still has to write down its reasons and publish that finding with the rule.
Quick recap: an agency can skip advance notice and comment if it finds, and explains, good cause that the normal process is impracticable, unnecessary, or against the public interest.

Once a rule is final, when does it kick in? Section 553 says the required publication or service of a substantive rule shall be made not less than 30 days before its effective date. That gives people time to prepare before a rule applies to them. But there are exceptions, including rules that grant an exemption or relieve a restriction, and cases where the agency finds good cause to set an earlier date. So the 30-day cushion is the default, not an absolute guarantee.
Quick recap: final substantive rules usually take effect no sooner than 30 days after publication, unless an exception or good cause applies.

What if someone thinks an agency got it wrong? Under 5 U.S.C. 706, a reviewing court shall hold unlawful and set aside agency action found to be arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law. Courts can also strike down agency action that's contrary to constitutional rights, or made without the procedures the law requires. This is the check that keeps agencies inside the boundaries Congress set, and it's why the notice, comment, and explanation steps we just covered matter so much in court.
Quick recap: courts can set aside agency action that is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise unlawful, including rules made without required procedures.

Let's see good cause used in real life. In February 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs published an interim final rule changing how it evaluates the effect of medication on a veteran's disability rating. VA said this regulation was needed immediately to minimize the negative impact of an erroneous line of cases, and said a recent court decision could require re-adjudicating over 350,000 pending claims. Because VA invoked good cause, the rule took effect the same day it was published, February 17, 2026, while comments stayed open until April 20. As of April 10, 2026, Regulations.gov showed 20,880 public comments on Regulations.gov, showing that even a rule that takes effect immediately can still draw a large public response.
Quick recap: VA used the good cause exception to make its medication-rating rule effective immediately, while still collecting public comments afterward.

That's the Administrative Procedure Act in a nutshell: what counts as a rule, how notice and comment works, when agencies can move fast under good cause, and how courts keep everyone honest. Thanks for learning with us today. Subscribe so you catch every episode of Rulemaking 101, and tell us in the comments about a rule you've followed or a question this raised for you. Then head to Regulations.gov and look for open proposed rules. Your comment becomes part of the record agencies must consider.
